title: Portfolio Phase 2: Chapters 6-10
descriptionMarkdown:
# Phase 2 — Issue tracker and priority index

## Graded checkpoint
Chapter 10 accepts id|priority|title records, rejects bad or repeated IDs, and sorts by descending priority with an ascending-ID tie-breaker. Preserve all different tasks even when priorities match. Error counts and order are part of the contract.

## Independent application
Build an in-memory issue tracker using records for transparent values, an enum for lifecycle, and a sealed result family where alternatives carry different data. Expose a repository role and implement it with collections chosen for actual operations. Add dependencies between issues and a traversal that identifies reachable prerequisites. Specify a policy for cycles rather than hanging indefinitely.

## Required evidence
- Equality and hashing tests for IDs used as map keys.
- Comparator tests with ties and extreme values; show why priority alone is not identity.
- A type-safe reusable helper without raw types or blanket unchecked suppressions.
- Complexity notes for lookup, ordered reports, dependency traversal, and insertion.
- Traces for empty input, duplicate records, disconnected nodes, and cycles.

## Review and completion
Demonstrate two repository implementations behind the same behavioral contract. A reviewer adds a workflow state or changes priority ordering; identify the affected code before editing it. Explain the cost of each data structure and defend composition versus inheritance. A passing index task does not assess the complete graph feature or architecture; those require repository review.
learningObjectives: Model closed workflow choices and transparent immutable issue values honestly
Substitute repository implementations while preserving equality, hashing, and ordering contracts
Use generics to preserve result and repository type relationships without raw types
Choose collections from ordering, uniqueness, lookup, mutation, and ownership requirements
Analyze and test search, sorting, dependency traversal, and worst-case behavior
